# Web — the server half

A LOGOS backend is a set of typed routes: one `## Route` per path, each declaring what it takes and
what it answers, and `Serve on port 8080.` to bind the port. The frontend is a set of pages that
compile to WebAssembly and call those routes — the [Frontend](frontend.md) guide covers it. One
project holds both, `largo serve` runs them together with hot reload, and `largo build --release`
packs pages, assets and backend into one native binary.

Nothing here is a framework binding. The HTTP helpers, the static-file server, the JSON reader, the
session cookies and the entire PostgreSQL wire protocol are written in LOGOS, in
[`assets/std/`](../crates/logicaffeine_compile/assets/std/), over a small set of socket primitives.
All of it can be read, and another protocol can be written the same way.

## The shape of a site

`largo new mysite --web` scaffolds three directories, by convention and with no extra manifest keys:

| Path | What it is |
|------|-----------|
| `src/main.lg` | The backend and its `Serve` statement |
| `pages/` | Pages, one WebAssembly bundle each; `app.lg` is served at `/` |
| `static/` | Files served verbatim at root-relative paths |

`largo new mysite --site` scaffolds `pages/` and `static/` alone: no backend, no `entry` in
`Largo.toml`, and a plain `largo build` exports it to `dist/` for a static host.

**One routing rule holds everywhere.** An exact match against a built page or a static asset wins;
anything else goes to the backend, whose route table matches it or answers `404`. The rule is the
same in development and inside the release binary.

```text
GET /style.css   ->  static/style.css             (asset, exact match)
GET /            ->  pages/app.lg                 (page, by convention)
GET /posts/7     ->  the route GET /posts/:id     (route, matched and bound)
GET /nope        ->  404                          (nothing matched)
```

## Routes

A site is a set of paths, so write one `## Route` per path. Each declares its method, its path, the
parameters it takes and the type it answers with; the router matches, binds and dispatches:

```logos
## Route GET / -> Text:
    Return "Hello from LOGOS".

## Route GET /posts/:id (id: Int) -> Text:
    Return "post {id}".

## Main
Serve on port 8080.
```

`Serve on port 8080.` binds the port and answers every request from the route table, once per
request and concurrently: a slow client cannot block another, and a failure in one request is a
`500` for that request rather than the end of the server. The port can be any expression, and
`LOGOS_PORT` or `PORT` in the environment overrides it, so the binary that serves 8080 on a laptop
takes the port a hosting platform assigns.

A route's parameters come from its own path. `:id` is a slot, `(id: Int)` names and types it, and a
segment that is not an `Int` is answered `400` rather than reaching the route. A parameter the path
has no slot for is bound from the query string, or from the body of a `POST` form. A route that
needs the whole request declares a `Request` parameter.

The answer type decides the content type, so a route says what it means rather than assembling a
header: `Text` is served as text, `View` is rendered as HTML, a record is encoded as JSON through
the codec derived from its declaration. A route that sets the status or a header answers
`Response` — which is also how a route sets a cookie, and so what makes [sessions](#sessions)
possible.

### Asking the route table

The same table answers questions without a socket, which is how a server is tested:

```logos
## Route GET /posts/:id (id: Int) -> Text:
    Return "post {id}".

## Route POST /echo (text: Text) -> Text:
    Return "you said {text}".

## Main
Show route("GET", "/posts/7").
Show routeStatus("GET", "/posts/seven").
Show routeWith("POST", "/echo", "text=hi").
Show routeContentType("GET", "/posts/7").
```

```output
post 7
400
you said hi
text/plain; charset=utf-8
```

`route(method, url)` answers the body a request would receive, `routeStatus` its status and
`routeContentType` its content type; `routeHeader(method, url, name)` reads one response header.
Each has a `…With(method, url, body)` form that sends a body. In a `## Test` they are ordinary
expressions:

```logos
## Route GET /health -> Text:
    Return "ok".

## Test: the health check answers

Expect that route("GET", "/health") is equal to "ok".
Expect that routeStatus("GET", "/missing") is equal to 404.
```

### Guards and redirects

`## Before each request (r: Request) -> Option of Response:` is a guard, and `## Redirect /old -> /new.`
moves a URL. Both belong to the route table:

```logos
## Before each request (r: Request) -> Option of Response:
    If r's path is equal to "/admin":
        Return some(unauthorized()).
    Return none.

## Redirect /old -> /new.

## Route GET /new -> Text:
    Return "here".

## Route GET /admin -> Text:
    Return "secret".

## Main
Show route("GET", "/admin").
Show routeStatus("GET", "/admin").
Show route("GET", "/old").
Show routeStatus("POST", "/old").
Show route("GET", "/new").
```

```output
Unauthorized
401
302 /new
302
here
```

A guard runs once per request, before the route table matches anything. `none` lets the request
through; `some(response)` is sent in the route's place — its own status, content type and headers —
and the route never runs. Guards run in the order they are declared, and the first to answer wins.
Because a guard runs before matching, it also answers a path no route declares and a path a redirect
moves, so an authorization check cannot be sidestepped by aiming at a URL that does not exist. The
guard's request carries the real headers and query; its `path` is the path without the query string,
so `/admin?x=1` is still `/admin` to it.

A redirect answers `302` with `Location` set, for every method, and a query string on the old URL
does not stop it matching. It never shadows a route: a path a `## Route` declares is served, not
redirected. Asked through the route table, a redirect's body is `302 /new`; the served response
carries the `Location` header.

### Taking the whole request by hand

`## Route` covers a site whose paths are known. A program that wants the dispatch itself — a proxy,
a catch-all, a path shape no pattern describes — writes one function from `Request` to `Response`
and serves with it:

```logos
## To handle (request: Request) -> Response:
    Let path be request's path.
    If path is equal to "/":
        Return html("<h1>Hello from LOGOS</h1>").
    If path is equal to "/api/health":
        Return json("{{\"ok\": true}}").
    Return notFound().

## Main
Serve on port 8080 with handle.
```

`Serve on port <expr> with <handler>` sends every request to that one function; the route table is
not consulted, no guard or redirect runs, and a `## Session` is not loaded or saved around it,
because all of them belong to the router's dispatch.

## The request

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `method` | `GET`, `POST`, and the rest, uppercase |
| `path` | The path, already percent-decoded, without the query string |
| `body` | The request body as text |
| `headers` | A map of header name to value |
| `query` | A map of query parameter to value |

Read headers with `headerOf`, which is case-insensitive because HTTP header names are, and query
parameters with `queryOf`, which is case-sensitive because query keys are. Both answer `""` for
something absent; `hasHeader` and `hasQuery` tell an absent key apart from an empty value.

`headerIn(headers, name)` is the same case-insensitive lookup against a header map rather than a
request. A request's headers and a response's headers are the same shape, so it reads a header off a
reply as well — `headerIn(reply's headers, "set-cookie")` — and `headerOf` is it applied to a
request.

A route that needs a query parameter declares it, and the router binds it; a route that needs the
headers or the raw body declares a `Request` parameter and reads them:

```logos
## Route GET /hello (name: Text) -> Text:
    Return "hello {name}".

## Route GET /agent (request: Request) -> Text:
    If hasHeader(request, "user-agent"):
        Return "agent: " + headerOf(request, "user-agent").
    Return "no agent".

## Main
Show route("GET", "/hello?name=ada").
```

```output
hello ada
```

## The response

A `Response` is a record of `status`, `contentType`, `body`, `bytes` and `headers`. `plain`, `html`
and `json` build a `200` with the matching content type. `notFound` builds a `404`.
`bytesResponse` carries raw bytes for binary content, which is how a compiled page or an image is
served.

Two refusals mean different things. `unauthorized` is a `401` — *I do not know who you are*, so
signing in will help. `forbidden` is a `403` — *I know who you are, and no*, so it will not. Sending
the wrong one leaves a signed-in visitor bouncing off a login page they are already past.
`redirectTo` sends a `302` with `Location` set; `permanentRedirectTo` sends a `301`, which asks every
cache on the way to remember the move — close to irreversible, so it is asked for by name.

Extra headers go on with `withHeader`, which returns a `Result` because four kinds of header are
refused rather than written: a name that is not a valid token, a value containing a control byte, a
hop-by-hop header the connection itself owns, and `content-type`, which belongs in the response's
own field. The refusal of control bytes is what stops response splitting at the source.

```logos
## Route GET /tagged -> Response:
    Inspect withHeader(plain("ok"), "x-app", "demo"):
        When Ok (r):
            Return r.
        When Err (message):
            Return plain(message).

## Main
Show routeHeader("GET", "/tagged", "x-app").
```

```output
demo
```

The rules it applies are callable on their own: `isHeaderName` for a whole name,
`isHeaderTokenByte` for one byte of one, `isHeaderValue` for a value with no control bytes, and
`isHopByHop` for the names the connection owns.

## Cookies

A cookie is how a session survives a request, which makes it the most security-sensitive header a
site emits. `cookie(name, value)` writes the safe attributes, and a program opts out rather than in:

```text
sid=abc123; Path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Secure
```

`HttpOnly` keeps a script from reading it, which is what makes an XSS a nuisance rather than an
account takeover. `SameSite=Lax` is what CSRF defence rests on: a cookie the browser will not attach
to a cross-site request cannot be replayed by another site's form. `Secure` keeps it off plaintext
HTTP.

A `Secure` cookie is never sent back over plain HTTP. `localhost` is exempt — browsers treat it as
trustworthy — but a LAN address is not, so a page opened on a phone at `http://192.168.1.20:8080`
signs in and then does not stay signed in. `cookieFor(name, value, secure)` says which it wants, and
`cookiesAreSecure()` is the answer `cookie` gives it: yes, unless `LOGOS_COOKIE_INSECURE` is set. The
default stays secure because the two mistakes differ in size: a missing `Secure` in production is a
session token in clear text on every request; an unwanted one in development is a sign-in that does
not stick. Dropping it drops only `Secure` — `HttpOnly` and `SameSite` defend against other attacks.

`withCookie(response, name, value)` sets one on a reply, `cookieOf(request, name)` reads one back
(the `Cookie` header is a list, so a page with several cookies works), and `expiredCookie(name)` is
how a sign-out deletes one: a zero lifetime is the only way to say *forget this*.

```logos
## Route POST /login -> Response:
    Return withCookie(plain("ok"), "sid", "ada").

## Route GET /me (request: Request) -> Text:
    Return cookieOf(request, "sid").

## Main
Show route("POST", "/login").
Show isCookieSafe("ada").
Show isCookieSafe("a;b").
```

```output
ok
true
false
```

A name or value containing `;`, a comma, a quote, a space or a control byte is **refused**: those
end the cookie, or the whole header, and everything after them becomes something nobody wrote —
response splitting, aimed at the session cookie. `isCookieSafe` is the check, callable first.
Refusing beats trimming: a silently truncated session id is a bug nobody can see.

## Sessions

A cookie is the mechanism; a session is what a program wants. Declare its fields and the router
does the rest:

```logos
## Session
    a user, which is Text.

## Route POST /login (name: Text) -> Response:
    Set the session's user to name.
    Return redirectTo("/").

## Route GET /me -> Text:
    Return the session's user.
```

`the session's user` is an ordinary possessive and reads and writes state that belongs to the
visitor and outlives the request. The router loads it from a signed cookie before anything
dispatches and saves it back **only when a request changed it**, so a read-only page sets no cookie
and a route that sets a cookie of its own is not overwritten.

Fields are `Text`, `Int` or `Bool`. A session travels in the cookie the browser sends with *every*
request, so it holds an id and the program looks the rest up from that.

A cookie is attacker-controlled input, so one whose signature does not check is not an error and
not a crash: it is a visitor with no session. `LOGOS_SESSION_SECRET` sets the signing key; with
nothing set the key is random per process, so sessions do not survive a restart, and a program
nobody configured still cannot have its sessions forged.

### CSRF

With a `## Session` declared, the router **checks the token itself** before a state-changing route
runs. A `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE` without a valid token is answered `403` and the route
never executes. A form carries the token in a `_csrf` field with `csrf()`:

```logos
## Session
    a user, which is Text.

## Route GET / -> View:
    <form method="post" action="/save">
      <input type="hidden" name="_csrf" value={csrf()}>
      <input name="title">
      <button>Save</button>
    </form>

## Route POST /save (title: Text) -> Text:
    Return "saved " + title.

## Main
Serve on port 8080.
```

The form is rendered by the server, the only place a per-visitor token can come from. A scripted
request sends the token as an `X-CSRF-Token` header instead of a form field.

The token is bound to a per-visitor nonce minted the first time `csrf()` is called on a visit — the
first moment that visitor needs a cookie, so one who never sees a form is never given one. A token
bound to the session's *contents* would hand every anonymous visitor the same token, and a token
every visitor shares is one an attacker reads off their own page.

Forgetting the field is a compile error: a `<form>` whose method changes state must carry a `_csrf`
field or the page does not build.

A page's own `POST`/`PUT`/`PATCH`/`DELETE` fetches to its own server carry the same token
automatically — no header to add by hand. The composing server writes the visitor's token into the
document as `<meta name="csrf-token">`, and every state-changing request the page's own code makes
to its own origin reads it from there and sends it as `x-csrf-token`; a request to another origin,
or a `GET`, is untouched. This is the wire the form field above rides for a plain `<form>` submit,
and the ONLY thing a scripted `fetch`-style request needs to add for the same protection is nothing.

### The primitives underneath

[`session.lg`](../crates/logicaffeine_compile/assets/std/session.lg) is what `## Session` is built
on, and a program that manages its own cookie calls it directly. `signSession(secret, value)` answers
the value followed by its HMAC-SHA-256 signature; `verifySession(secret, cookie)` answers
`some value` when the signature checks and `none` for anything else, never trapping on a malformed
cookie. `sessionMac(cookie)` is the signature half, for a program that inspects it. The signature is split at the *last* separator, so a value may itself contain `|` without
letting an attacker move the boundary. `csrfToken(secret, session)` and `csrfValid(secret, session,
token)` bind a CSRF token to one session under a key distinct from the cookie's. `sessionSecret()`
reads `LOGOS_SESSION_SECRET` and falls back to `randomSecret()`. A payload of several fields is
hex-encoded per field and joined with `.` — `hexText` and `unhexText` convert, and
`sessionField(payload, i)`, `sessionInt` and `sessionBool` read field `i`, counting from 1, answering
the empty value for a field an older cookie does not carry.

## Static files

`largo serve` and the release binary serve `static/` without a line of code. A program that serves
files itself — downloads under their own prefix, say — uses `staticUnder`, which refuses any path
containing a `..` segment before a byte reaches the disk and answers `404` for a file that is not
there. `fileResponse` serves one known path.

```logos
## Route GET /downloads/:name (name: Text) -> Response:
    Return staticUnder("downloads", name).

## Main
Show routeStatus("GET", "/downloads/..%2F..%2Fetc%2Fpasswd").
Show hasTraversal("../../etc/passwd").
```

```output
404
true
```

A refused traversal and an absent file give the same `404`, so a prober learns nothing from the
difference. `hasTraversal` is the guard itself, for a path built from parts.

`contentTypeFor` maps an extension to a MIME type, and it is **the** MIME table: `largo serve` and
`largo build` read this function rather than keeping their own, so a file is typed identically in
development and production. Text types name their charset (`text/css; charset=utf-8`), because a
browser guessing an encoding renders a visitor's name as mojibake; `text/javascript` is the exception
its own specification asks for. An unknown extension is `application/octet-stream` — a download,
never a guess, since guessing `text/html` would let an uploaded file be served as a page.

## Reading JSON

A route that answers a record is encoded for you, and a route parameter of a record type is decoded
for you. For JSON read by hand, `jsonTryParse` is lenient the way a browser is — a duplicate object
key keeps the last value — and `jsonParseStrict` rejects duplicate keys with a positioned message,
which is what anything deciding money or access wants. Both return a `JsonResult`.

A brace in a text literal opens an interpolation hole, so a hand-written JSON object doubles its
braces and escapes its quotes: `"{{\"ok\": true}}"` is the text `{"ok": true}`. Text that arrives in a
request body needs no escaping.

```logos
## Main
Let parsed be jsonParseStrict("{{\"ok\": true}}").
Inspect parsed:
    When JOk (value):
        Show "ok".
    When JErr (message):
        Show message.
```

```output
ok
```

Pull typed values out with `jsonField`, `jsonString`, `jsonInt`, `jsonBool` and `jsonArray`. Each
returns a `Result`, so an authorization decision is never made on a field that was the wrong type or
missing. `jsonField` distinguishes an absent key from one stored as null. `jsonRequireObject` insists
the value is an object, and `jsonNoExtraKeys` closes the shape so an extra field cannot be smuggled
past the decoder.

## Rendering HTML on the server

A route answering `View` is a template, rendered on the server with every hole escaped, and a
component renders to text with `html of`:

```logos
## Component Greeting
State:
    Let name be "ada".
View:
    <p>Hi {name}</p>

## Main
Show html of Greeting.
```

```output
<p>Hi ada</p>
```

A server-rendered page is the page a browser would paint, serialized: every hole in an attribute
is escaped as `htmlEscape` escapes it and every hole in text as `htmlEscapeText` does, and a URL
attribute a browser follows goes through `safeUrl`. The two escapers are needed by hand only when
building markup as text.

`htmlEscape` replaces the four characters that mean something to an HTML parser — `&` first, or the
entities it adds would be re-escaped, then `<`, `>` and `"`. The quote is there because the same
function guards attribute values, where a bare quote ends the attribute. `htmlEscapeText` replaces
three: between tags a `"` ends nothing, and escaping it would make the bytes a server sends differ
from the bytes a browser paints, which every cross-tier comparison in this codebase reads.

```logos
## Main
Show htmlEscape("<b>hi</b>").
Show htmlEscape("a\"b").
Show htmlEscapeText("a\"b").
```

```output
&lt;b&gt;hi&lt;/b&gt;
a&quot;b
a"b
```

`safeUrl` guards a URL that becomes an `href`, a `src`, an `action` or any attribute a browser
follows. Escaping does nothing to `javascript:alert(1)` — it holds none of the characters
`htmlEscape` replaces — so `safeUrl` answers `"about:blank#blocked"` for a URL whose scheme executes,
and the URL itself otherwise, after normalising the case, whitespace and control characters a
browser ignores when it reads a scheme.

```logos
## Main
Show safeUrl("/todos/1").
Show safeUrl("java\tscript:alert(1)").
```

```output
/todos/1
about:blank#blocked
```

## URLs, query strings and form bodies

A route binds its parameters from the path, the query and the body. These are the functions it
uses, for the times a URL is read by hand.

`isIntText` asks whether text reads as a whole number. `parseInt` traps on text that is not one,
which is right for a program reading its own data and wrong for a server reading a stranger's URL;
the router asks first, which is why `/posts/abc` is a `400`. `""` and a lone `"-"` are rejected as
firmly as `"abc"`.

`pathOf` is everything before the first `?` — what a route matches on — and `queryString` everything
after it. `queryParam` reads one named parameter out of a query, and `urlDecode` undoes the encoding
a browser applies (`+` is a space, `%XX` is a byte; `hexDigitValue` is the digit reader underneath).
Decoding works over bytes, because percent-encoding encodes bytes: a check mark arrives as
`%E2%9C%93`. A `%` not followed by two hex digits is left alone — `50%` is text somebody typed.

A `POST` form puts its parameters in the body, and a scripted post puts JSON there. `bodyParam`
reads a named value out of either, deciding by the first character. Going the other way, `urlEncode`
escapes a value for a query string or a form body: it leaves the unreserved characters alone
(`isUnreservedByte` is its test, per RFC 3986) and percent-escapes every other byte, with
`hexByteText` writing one as `%XX`. `charAtText(s, i)` reads the character at a **1-based** byte
offset — it is the digit-table lookup under `hexByteText`, where the offset is a digit's value plus
one — and answers `""` past the end.

```logos
## Main
Show isIntText("42").
Show isIntText("4a").
Show pathOf("/search?q=hi").
Show queryString("/search?q=hi").
Show queryParam("q=hello+world&page=3", "q").
Show urlDecode("a%2Fb").
Show bodyParam("text=buy%20milk", "text").
Show urlEncode("buy milk").
Show charAtText("abc", 3).
```

```output
true
false
/search
q=hi
hello world
a/b
buy milk
buy%20milk
c
```

An upload is not a plain `POST`: it is `multipart/form-data`, and three functions build it.
`multipartBoundary` derives a delimiter that cannot occur inside the content it delimits — a random
one would make every recorded request unreproducible, and a colliding one would truncate the upload
at that byte. `multipartBody` frames the part with CRLF line endings, and `multipartContentType`
names the boundary in the header; they are produced in different places, so a mismatch fails every
upload on a real server while passing a test that reads only one of them.

## Storing data

[`postgres.lg`](../crates/logicaffeine_compile/assets/std/postgres.lg) speaks the PostgreSQL version 3
wire protocol in LOGOS over the socket primitives: cleartext, MD5 and SCRAM-SHA-256 authentication,
the simple and extended query protocols, transactions, statement timeouts and query cancellation.

`pgConnect` opens a connection from a URL and `pgClose` ends it. `pgConnectSecure` takes the same URL
and negotiates TLS first — a server that declines is refused rather than spoken to in the clear.
Hosted databases (RDS, Neon, Supabase, Cloud SQL) reject an unencrypted connection, so `pgConnect`
reaches a database on your own machine and `pgConnectSecure` reaches a managed one; everything after
the connection is identical. `pgQuery` runs a statement and returns rows; `pgExecute` runs one that
returns none and answers the number of rows affected. For a statement run many times, `pgPrepare`
parses it on the server and `pgExecPrepared` runs it with fresh arguments.

**Put user data in parameters, never in SQL text.** `pgQueryParams` sends the statement and its
arguments as separate wire fields, so nothing a user types is read as SQL. The only SQL the module
composes itself comes from a closed, validated set.

```logos
## To insertNote (pgc: PgConn) and (body: Text) -> Bool:
    Let params be a new Seq of Text.
    Push body to params.
    Let done be pgQueryParams(pgc, "INSERT INTO notes (body) VALUES ($1)", params).
    Inspect done:
        When Ok (result):
            Return true.
        When Err (message):
            Return false.
```

Read cells with `pgTextAt`, `pgIntAt`, `pgBoolAt`, `pgRealAt`, and the typed `pgDecimalAt`,
`pgUuidAt` and `pgEnumAt`. NULL is honest: the option-returning variants (`pgTextAtOpt` and its
siblings) answer `none`, and `pgIsNullAt` asks directly, while the plain getters surface NULL as an
empty string. Use the option getters wherever NULL is meaningful.

A connection is one socket holding one strictly ordered conversation. Run one statement at a time on
it and open more connections for parallelism; there is no pool in this version.

## Raw sockets

Everything above stands on [`tcp.lg`](../crates/logicaffeine_compile/assets/std/tcp.lg):
`tcpConnect`, `tcpSend`, `tcpRecv`, `tcpRecvExact` and `tcpClose` on the client side, `tcpListen`,
`tcpAccept` and `tcpListenerPort` on the server side, plus `tcpShutdownWrite` and `tcpSetTimeout`. A
connection is an opaque integer handle, bytes travel as a sequence of integers, and every operation
returns a `Result`, so a network failure is a value rather than a trap. A clean close reads as an
empty result from `tcpRecv`, while `tcpRecvExact` treats an early close as an error, which is what a
framed protocol needs.

`tcpConnectTls` dials a host and completes a TLS handshake before returning, and `tcpUpgradeTls`
turns an established plain connection into an encrypted one in place — what a protocol that
negotiates first requires: PostgreSQL sends an eight-byte request, reads a one-byte answer, and only
then hands the socket to TLS. Both return the same handle, so `tcpSend`, `tcpRecv` and `tcpClose`
work unchanged. Certificates are checked against the Mozilla root set bundled into the binary, so a
build behaves the same wherever it runs; `LOGOS_TLS_EXTRA_ROOT` names a PEM file to trust in
addition, for a private certificate authority or a test server.

## Hashing and passwords

[`crypto.lg`](../crates/logicaffeine_compile/assets/std/crypto.lg) carries `sha256`, `hmacSha256` and
`pbkdf2Sha256` as LOGOS source, pinned to the FIPS 180-4, RFC 4231 and RFC 7677 vectors. They take and
return sequences of bytes. The interpreted tiers accelerate the key derivation natively because it is
deliberately expensive; the compiled tiers build the LOGOS source; both are locked to the same
vectors.

## Running and deploying

```bash
largo new mysite --web
cd mysite
largo serve
```

`largo serve` owns the public port, serves the pages and assets from memory, and proxies the rest to
the backend running as a child process. It watches all three directories: editing a page or an asset
rebuilds it and reloads the browser, and editing the backend restarts the child. A site with no
backend is published with `largo build --static`, covered in the [Frontend](frontend.md#building-and-deploying)
guide, as is `## Error page`.

`largo build --release` produces one native binary with the pages, the assets and the backend
embedded:

```bash
largo build --release
PORT=8080 ./target/release/mysite
```

That binds `127.0.0.1`, so running a program does not publish it to the network. Inside a container,
behind a load balancer, or anywhere traffic arrives from another host, name the interface:

```bash
LOGOS_HOST=0.0.0.0 PORT=8080 ./mysite
```

`LOGOS_HOST` takes an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address (bracketed for you) or a hostname. The server
speaks HTTP; terminate TLS in front of it — nginx, Caddy, or whatever the platform puts in front of a
container.

### In production

A server built this way refuses a request rather than queueing it when it is already serving as many
as it will, bounds how long a handler may run and how long a client may take to send, and on a stop
signal stops accepting, finishes the work it has, and releases the port. Every bound is read from the
environment in one place, so the same names work on every tier:

| Variable | What it bounds |
|----------|----------------|
| `LOGOS_HOST` | The interface to bind. Defaults to `127.0.0.1` |
| `LOGOS_MAX_INFLIGHT` | How many requests may be served at once before the rest are refused |
| `LOGOS_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS` | How long one handler may run |
| `LOGOS_READ_DEADLINE_MS` | How long a client may take to finish sending |
| `LOGOS_DRAIN_MS` | How long a graceful stop waits for in-flight work |
| `LOGOS_MAX_BODY` | The largest request body accepted; a larger one is answered `413` |
| `LOGOS_READY_PATH` | A path answering a readiness probe. Unset by default |
| `LOGOS_HEALTH_PATH` | A path answering a liveness probe. Unset by default |
| `LOGOS_CORRELATION_ID` | `1`, `true`, `yes` or `on`: every response carries an `X-Correlation-Id` — the client's own, else one the server assigns |

Readiness reports whether the server wants traffic and turns `503` the moment it starts draining.
Liveness reports only that the process is answering and stays `200` through a drain, so an
orchestrator stops sending work without killing a server that is still finishing some. With neither
named no path is reserved, so the route table keeps every path it declares.

On the interpreted tier the request budget is checked between statements, so it bounds a runaway loop
rather than a single long-running builtin. The compiled tier races a real timer.

A request body is framed by `Content-Length` alone: a request sent with `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`
is answered `400`, as is any request whose bytes do not parse.

A compiled binary serves on one of two engines, and says which on stderr when it starts. On Linux
it defaults to a thread-per-core io_uring engine wherever the kernel can set up a ring, and to tokio
everywhere else; the interpreted tier always serves on tokio. The io_uring engine runs a handler
inline on its shard's thread, so it cannot bound a handler's time, shed by admission or answer a
probe path: setting `LOGOS_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS`, `LOGOS_MAX_INFLIGHT`, `LOGOS_READY_PATH`,
`LOGOS_HEALTH_PATH` or `LOGOS_CORRELATION_ID` moves the binary onto tokio, naming the variable that
did it, so the guarantee asked for holds. `LOGOS_MAX_BODY` and `LOGOS_READ_DEADLINE_MS` are enforced
by both engines.

| Variable | What it selects |
|----------|-----------------|
| `LOGOS_HTTP_ENGINE` | `uring` or `tokio`, overriding the default; `uring` where no ring can be set up falls back to tokio and says why |
| `LOGOS_HTTP_SHARDS` | The io_uring engine's shard count. Defaults to one per core |
| `LOGOS_HTTP_ACCESS_LOG` | Any value: the tokio engine prints one `logos-http method=… path=… status=… correlation_id=… dur_ms=…` line per request to stderr, never a header value |

## Where this is tested

The examples above run as part of the documentation suite, and each output shown is checked against
the program's real output. The behaviour they describe is pinned by `route_request_response_lock`,
`server_surface_lock` for guards, redirects and error pages, `session_lock`, `csrf_automatic_lock`
for the router's token check, `http_static_lock`, `json_conformance_lock` and `json_typed_decode_lock`,
`http_lifecycle_lock` and `http_lifecycle_bounds_lock` for the production bounds, `http_engine_fallback`
for the engine choice,
`postgres_wire` and `postgres_protocol` against recorded wire transcripts, `postgres_live` against a
real PostgreSQL server, `tcp_natives` and `tcp_cross_tier`, `http_workers` for concurrent serving,
`crypto_sha2_lock` for the digest vectors, and `http_differential`, which asserts the interpreted and
compiled servers answer the same request with byte-identical bytes.

# Logic mode — English → First-Order Logic

English lets one sentence mean two things and never says which: *every woman loves a man* can mean
one man loved by all of them, or a man for each. Logic mode parses English into First-Order Logic,
where each meaning is its own formula a machine can check. It is deterministic: where a sentence is
genuinely ambiguous, LOGOS can return *every* reading rather than guessing one. It also parses
*strictly*: a sentence whose words can't all be consumed fails with a `TrailingTokens` error rather
than yielding a silent partial reading, so dropped meaning is a bug, not a style nit.

After this guide you can call the API, read the shape of its output, and find the phase test that
pins any construction. Every example below is produced by the compiler itself.

```rust
let fol = logicaffeine_language::compile("Every man is mortal.")?;
// → "∀x((Man(x) → Mortal(x)))"
```

## The API

| Function | Signature | Notes |
|----------|-----------|-------|
| `compile` | `(&str) -> Result<String, ParseError>` | one reading |
| `compile_forest` | `(&str) -> Vec<String>` | every reading (infallible), up to `MAX_FOREST_READINGS` |
| `compile_all_scopes` | `(&str) -> Result<Vec<String>, ParseError>` | the distinct quantifier-scope readings |
| `compile_with_options` | `(&str, CompileOptions) -> Result<String, ParseError>` | choose the output format / pragmatics |

Output formats (`OutputFormat`): **Unicode** (default), **LaTeX**, **SimpleFOL**, and **Kripke**
(modals lowered to explicit world quantification). `compile_pragmatic` adds scalar implicatures as
a separate, cancellable line. From the terminal, [`largo logic`](cli.md#logic) takes the sentence
inline, from `--file`, or from stdin, with `--format unicode|latex|ascii|kripke`,
`--all-readings`, `--pragmatic` and `--discourse` (one sentence per line, shared anaphora).

## The shape of the output

LOGOS does not stop at surface predicates. Two features show up throughout:

- **Neo-Davidsonian event semantics** — verbs introduce an event variable `e` with explicit
  thematic roles (`Agent`, `Theme`, `Past`, …):

  ```
  "John loved Mary."
  → ∃e(Love(e) ∧ Agent(e, John) ∧ Theme(e, Mary) ∧ Past(e))
  ```

- **Ontology expansion** — nouns carry their semantic class, so a *dog* is also an *animal* and a
  *mammal*:

  ```
  "Every dog barks."
  → ∀x((((Dog(x) ∧ Animal(x)) ∧ Mammal(x)) → ∃e(Bark(e) ∧ Agent(e, x))))
  ```

## Quantifiers

```
"Some cat sleeps."
→ ∃x((((Cat(x) ∧ Animal(x)) ∧ Mammal(x)) ∧ ∃e(Sleep(e) ∧ Agent(e, x))))

"No bird flies."
→ ∀x(((Bird(x) ∧ Animal(x)) → ¬∃e(Fly(e) ∧ Agent(e, x))))
```

Universal (`every`, `all`, `each`), existential (`some`, `a`, `an`), negative (`no`, `none`),
proportional (`most`, `few`, `many`), counted (`three`, `at least three`, `at most three`),
infinitary and generic readings are all handled (`QuantifierKind` in `ast/logic.rs`). A determiner
reads the same way in every construction it heads: it fixes the quantifier and how the restrictor
meets the scope — `R → S` under `all` and `all but finitely many`, `R → ¬S` under `no`, `R ∧ S`
under the rest.

### Infinitary quantifiers

`infinitely many` is Mostowski's quantifier ∃^∞, `finitely many` (or `only finitely many`) is
∃^<∞, and `all but finitely many` is the cofinite quantifier ∀^∞:

```
"Infinitely many primes are odd."
→ ∃^∞x((Primes(x) ∧ Odd(x)))

"All but finitely many dogs bark."
→ ∀^∞x((((Dog(x) ∧ Animal(x)) ∧ Mammal(x)) → ∃e(Bark(e) ∧ Agent(e, x))))
```

LaTeX writes them `\exists^{\infty}`, `\exists^{<\infty}` and `\forall^{\infty}`. The proof
engine reads them over the order of the naturals, where a set is infinite exactly when it is
unbounded: ∃^∞x φ is ∀b ∃x (x > b ∧ φ), ∀^∞x φ is ∃b ∀x (x > b → φ), and ∃^<∞x φ is
∃b ∀x (x > b → ¬φ).

`infinitely often` is G F, at either end of the sentence, and `eventually, always` is its dual F G:

```
"The light flashes infinitely often."
→ G(F(∃x(((Light(x) ∧ ∀y((Light(y) → y = x))) ∧ HAB(∃e(Flash(e) ∧ Agent(e, x)))))))
```

`x is infinitely close to y` is the relation `InfinitelyClose(x, y)` of nonstandard analysis.

## Connectives & negation

`and` (∧), `or` (∨), `if…then` (→), `iff` (↔), and `not` (¬). `and` binds tighter than `or`.

```
"John does not run."
→ ¬HAB(∃e(Run(e) ∧ Agent(e, John)))
```

(`HAB` is the habitual-aspect operator; see Tense & aspect below.)

## Modality

Modal verbs lower to Kripke-style modal operators with a force value (`□` necessity, `◇`
possibility), over alethic / deontic / temporal domains.

```
"Every student must study."
→ ∀x((Student(x) → □_{1.0} ∃e(Study(e) ∧ Agent(e, x))))
```

Use `OutputFormat::Kripke` to lower modals to explicit world quantification.

## Tense & aspect

Past/future tense and progressive / perfect / habitual / iterative aspect are tracked (Prior-style
operators plus LTL operators for hardware temporal logic). `"John loved Mary."` carries `Past(e)`;
present-tense generics carry `HAB`.

## Comparatives

```
"John is taller than Mary."
→ Taller(John, Mary)
```

Degree semantics covers comparatives, superlatives and equatives.

## Relative clauses

```
"The man who owns a dog is happy."
→ ∃x(((Man(x) ∧ (((Dog(y) ∧ Animal(y)) ∧ Mammal(y)) ∧ ∃e(Own(e) ∧ Agent(e, x) ∧ Theme(e, y)))) ∧ Happy(x)))
```

## Arithmetic sentences

A quantified arithmetic sentence has its own term layer
([`parser/math.rs`](../crates/logicaffeine_language/src/parser/math.rs)): `plus`, `minus`, `times`
and `divided by` are `Add`, `Sub`, `Mul` and `Div`, a lowercase-leading name is a variable (bound
when the `For all` prefix names it), an uppercase- or digit-leading name is a constant, a number
word is a numeral in any case, and `f(n)` is a function term.

```
"For all n, n plus 0 equals n."
→ ∀n(Add(n, 0) = n)

"For all a b, a plus b equals b plus a."
→ ∀a(∀b(Add(a, b) = Add(b, a)))

"For all but finitely many n, n plus 0 equals n."
→ ∀^∞n(Add(n, 0) = n)
```

A binder outranks the numeral table (`For all one, one times one equals one.` binds `one`), and a
numeral too large for `i64` travels as its own spelling rather than a rounded float. These are the
sentences a `## Theorem` proves with the ring oracle; see
[Proof & verification](proof-and-verification.md#arithmetic-in-english).

## Reciprocals & plurals

A reciprocal is symmetric, so it is genuinely ambiguous — `compile` returns *both* numbered readings
rather than guessing:

```
"John and Mary love each other."
→ 1) Love(John, Mary)  2) Love(Mary, John)
```

Plurals follow the verb: a distributive verb (*sleep*) applies to each member, a collective one
(*gather*) to the group, and a mixed one (*lift*) yields both readings from `compile_forest`.

## Scope ambiguity

When a sentence has more than one reading, `compile_forest` / `compile_all_scopes` return them all
instead of committing to one. This is the determinism guarantee in practice.

```rust
let readings = logicaffeine_language::compile_forest("Every man loves a woman.");
// → surface scope (∀ > ∃) and inverse scope (∃ > ∀); compile_forest is infallible
```

Here are both readings of the sentence this guide opened with, exactly as `compile_all_scopes` returns them
(and as `largo logic --all-readings "Every woman loves a man."` prints them):

```
"Every woman loves a man."
1. ∀x((Woman(x) → ∃y((Man(y) ∧ ∃e(Love(e) ∧ Agent(e, x) ∧ Theme(e, y))))))
2. ∃y((Man(y) ∧ ∀x((Woman(x) → ∃e(Love(e) ∧ Agent(e, x) ∧ Theme(e, y))))))
```

Reading 1 lets each woman love a different man; reading 2 says there is one man every woman loves. Neither is
the "right" one, so neither is dropped.

## The long tail

LOGOS covers a wide range of linguistic phenomena, each pinned by a phase test in
[`crates/logicaffeine_tests/tests/`](../crates/logicaffeine_tests/tests/):

| Phenomenon | Test file |
|------------|-----------|
| Garden-path sentences | `phase1_garden_path` |
| Wh-questions | `phase5_wh_movement`, `phase_question_answer` |
| Ellipsis / sluicing / gapping | `phase10_ellipsis`, `phase10b_sluicing`, `phase132_gapping` |
| Event semantics & thematic roles | `phase65_event_semantics`, `phase41_event_adjectives` |
| Higher-order / λ-calculus (Montague) | `phase66_higher_order` |
| Presupposition projection | `phase113_presupposition_projection`, `phase142_vandersandt` |
| Counterfactual conditionals | `phase110_counterfactuals` |
| Binding & coreference | `phase114_binding_theory`, `phase143_binding` |
| Scalar implicature & focus | `phase130_implicature`, `phase120_clefts` |
| Causality / concession | `phase122_causal_concessive` |
| Mass vs count | `phase115_mass_count` |
| Metaphor / metonymy / deixis / vagueness | `phase11_metaphor`, `phase129_metonymy`, `phase128_deixis`, `phase127_vagueness` |
| Discourse / anaphora (multi-sentence) | `phase42_drs`, `phase45_session` (the `Session` API) |

The test suite is the living specification: when in doubt about what a construction yields, the
phase test shows the exact output.

## See also

- The implementation crate → [`logicaffeine_language`](../crates/logicaffeine_language/README.md)
- The proof side (what you can *do* with the logic) → [Proof & verification](proof-and-verification.md)

## Where this is tested

The code is in [`crates/logicaffeine_language/`](../crates/logicaffeine_language/): the lexer
([`lexer.rs`](../crates/logicaffeine_language/src/lexer.rs)), the parser modules
([`parser/`](../crates/logicaffeine_language/src/parser/)), the AST
([`ast/logic.rs`](../crates/logicaffeine_language/src/ast/logic.rs)), and the transpiler
([`transpile.rs`](../crates/logicaffeine_language/src/transpile.rs)). Every `"English" → FOL` pair
in this guide is checked against the live compiler by `doc_examples`.

Beyond the long-tail table above, each section's phenomena are held by:

- Quantifiers: `phase20_axioms`, `phase112_partitive_quantifiers`, `phase117_cumulative`,
  `logic_determiner_readings`, `logic_infinitary_quantifiers`.
- Connectives & negation: `phase2_polarity`, `phase15_negation`.
- Modality: `phase139_modal_frames`, `phase123_evidentials`, `phase125_optatives`.
- Tense & aspect: `phase3_time`, `phase3_aspect`, `phase16_aspect`, `phase_hw_temporal`.
- Comparatives: `phase8_degrees`, `phase17_degrees`, `phase119_equatives`, `phase126_degree_standard`.
- Relative clauses: `phase5_wh_movement`, `phase135_appositive_rc`.
- Arithmetic sentences: `L_language_extra`.
- Reciprocals & plurals: `phase4_reciprocals`, `phase18_plurality`, `phase19_group_plurals`,
  `phase44_distributive`.
- Scope ambiguity: `phase12_ambiguity`, `phase116_island_scope`.

# Concurrency & distributed systems

A concurrency bug that shows up once in a thousand runs is a bug you cannot fix, because you cannot
watch it happen twice. LOGOS treats concurrency, message passing, replicated state, and networking
as first-class language features, and backs them with a deterministic runtime: a seed or a recorded
trace fixes every scheduling choice, so a failing run replays exactly. They run across native and
browser targets.

After this guide you can launch tasks and join them, pass messages through pipes and agents,
declare replicated types that merge without conflicts, sync them over the network, and replay a
failing concurrent run.

## The runtime

[`logicaffeine_runtime`](../crates/logicaffeine_runtime/README.md) is a **deterministic** scheduler:
pure `std`, tokio-free, and WASM-safe (the **Lamport invariant** keeps the data layer IO-free).
Scheduling decisions come from a `Chooser` driven by a seed (`SchedSeed`) or a recorded trace
(`SchedTrace`), so a concurrent run is **reproducible and replayable** (`run_with_seed`,
`run_with_trace`). There are two drivers behind one model:

- **Cooperative M:1** (the WASM path): single-threaded, deterministic.
- **Work-stealing M:N** (native, `cfg(not(wasm32))`): genuine multicore.

The runtime is used by the interpreter/VM tiers; an AOT-compiled binary is never linked against it.
A default `largo build` lowers tasks, pipes and select to host primitives through
[`logicaffeine_system`](../crates/logicaffeine_system/README.md) (`tokio::spawn`, tokio channels,
`tokio::select!`, rayon or OS threads for `Simultaneously:`, libp2p for the mesh) and runs them
free. A deterministic build, through the library entry points `compile_to_rust_deterministic` and
`compile_program_full_deterministic`, instead runs every task, pipe, timer and select on
[`logicaffeine_system::replay`](../crates/logicaffeine_system/src/replay.rs). That is the runtime's
scheduler ported step for step onto Rust futures, drawing each choice from the same seeded chooser,
so the binary run at `LOGOS_SEED=s` prints what the interpreter prints at seed `s`.

The C family carries a port too. Host C, RISC-V, the bytecode walker and the CUDA tier carry the
runtime's scheduler with them, ported to C (`codegen_c/sched_core.c`) one operation at a time, so a
compiled binary interleaves its tasks exactly as the interpreter does:

- a launched task runs before its parent resumes;
- every pipe operation is a scheduling point;
- a default pipe holds 32 values;
- a task left waiting forever is a deadlock.

Each binary draws its choices from the seed in `LOGOS_SEED`, read the same way the interpreter
reads it.
Host C and RISC-V run each task as a coroutine on a stack of its own; the bytecode walker and the
GPU run it as a step function over a heap frame, the form a GPU thread can run. A GPU thread cannot
unwind, so on the GPU a failure inside a runtime helper (a zero divisor, an index out of range)
stops the whole run; a failing `Require` fails only its task, as everywhere else.

The direct WASM backend carries no scheduler: a launched task runs to completion at its launch, a pipe
is a FIFO queue, `Sleep` advances nothing and `Close` has no observable effect. That is the
scheduler's order for a program whose tasks never block.

## Structured concurrency

```logos
## Main
Attempt all of the following:      # async / I/O-bound — joined
    Show "fetch A".
    Show "fetch B".
Simultaneously:                    # CPU-bound — run in parallel
    Show "crunch X".
    Show "crunch Y".
```

The two blocks are the `Concurrent` and `Parallel` statements in `ast/stmt.rs`.

## Tasks, channels & select

Green threads and Go-style channels (`Pipe`). A producer task feeds a consumer:

```logos
## To produce (ch: Int):
    Send 1 into ch.
    Send 2 into ch.

## Main
    Let jobs be a Pipe of Int.
    Launch a task to produce with jobs.
    Receive first from jobs.
    Receive second from jobs.
    Show first.
    Show second.
```

A task gets a copy of each value it is launched with, as a pipe's receiver gets a copy of what was sent:
a list the task changes is its own. A task may run on a worker thread of its own, so a value that
cannot leave the program's thread — a function, or a real number a function of the program defines —
stops the program where it is launched with it or sent.

`Select` waits on whichever arm is ready first, a receive or a timeout:

```logos
Await the first of:
    Receive x from jobs:
        Show x.
    After 1 seconds:
        Show "timeout".
```

A closed pipe keeps what was sent to it: its buffered values are still received, in order, and a
receive after the last one yields `nothing`:

```logos
## Main
Let ch be a Pipe of Int.
Send 5 into ch.
Close ch.
Receive a from ch.
Receive b from ch.
Show a.
Show b.
```

```output
5
nothing
```

A task handle is joined with `Await h.` (or `Wait for h.`), which parks until the task finishes:

```logos
## To slow:
    Sleep 4.
    Show "slow done".

## Main
Let h be Launch a task to slow.
Show "awaiting".
Await h.
Show "joined".
```

```output
awaiting
slow done
joined
```

The full set: `LaunchTask` (`Launch a task to <fn> with <args>`), `LaunchTaskWithHandle`
(`Let h be Launch a task to <fn>`), `StopTask` (`Stop h.`), `AwaitTask` (`Await h.` / `Wait for h.`,
optionally `… into r`), `CreatePipe` (`Let ch be a Pipe of T`), `SendPipe`/`ReceivePipe` and their
`Try…` variants (`Try to send <v> into ch`), `CloseChannel` (`Close ch.` / `Close the pipe ch.`), and
`Select`. The scheduler does not carry a task's return value back, so `Await h into r.` binds `r` to
`nothing`. Every one runs on the tree-walker and the VM (channel, spawn, await and select opcodes),
on the C family, and in a deterministic build.

## Agents (message passing)

```logos
Spawn a Worker called "w1".
Send Ping to "w1".
Await response from "w1" into reply.
```

Messages can be `compressed` (Lz4/Deflate/Zstd), `cached` (schema dictionary), or `unchecked`
(latency trade-off). `shared` ships a struct as a type id both ends derive from the same program,
`indexed` (`addressable`) lays a record list out for O(1) random field reads, `deduped` sends a
repeated subtree once with back-references, and `computed` ships a pure one-argument function as a
sandboxed computation. `Send unreliably <msg> to <peer>` marks the message a best-effort, unordered
datagram (`SendMessage.unreliable`); every tier delivers it as a reliable send. The three verbs are
the `Spawn`, `SendMessage` and `AwaitMessage` statements.

A `Send` can also choose a **wire layout**: a size↔speed↔resilience dial the sender picks for its
link, orthogonal to the modifiers above.

| Word | Layout | For |
|------|--------|-----|
| `fast` / `quickly` | fixed-width (memcpy) | latency-bound / fat links (LAN, datacenter, RDMA) |
| `compact` / `small` | varint (the default) | mobile / WAN / metered |
| `packed` | SIMD group-varint | the balanced middle |
| `smallest` / `best` | per-column compression menu | bandwidth-bound, CPU cheap |
| `redundant` / `tough` | Reed-Solomon FEC shards | lossy / one-way links (UDP, multicast, BLE, LoRa) — reconstruct from any *K* |

```logos
Send redundant Ping to "w1".   # survives shard loss with no retransmit
```

The `redundant` layout splits the message into Reed-Solomon shards
([`concurrency/fec.rs`](../crates/logicaffeine_compile/src/concurrency/fec.rs)). The modifiers and
the layout menu (`ast::SendLayout`) are applied by the tree-walker's relay send; the VM, AOT-Rust and
C lower `Send` to a plain message send and ignore them. The wire is self-describing, so a peer
decodes either form.

## CRDTs

[`logicaffeine_data/src/crdt/`](../crates/logicaffeine_data/src/crdt/) defines the conflict-free
replicated types, all sharing a `Merge` trait and causal metadata (dots, vector clocks), with delta
support where applicable:

| CRDT | File | What it is |
|------|------|-----------|
| `GCounter` | `gcounter.rs` | Grow-only counter |
| `PNCounter` | `pncounter.rs` | Increment/decrement counter |
| `LWWRegister` | `lww.rs` | Last-write-wins register |
| `MVRegister` | `mvregister.rs` | Multi-value register (concurrent writes = conflict set) |
| `ORSet` | `orset.rs` | Observed-remove set (add-wins / remove-wins bias) |
| `ORMap` | `ormap.rs` | Observed-remove map |
| `LatestWrite` | `latest.rs` | Last-writer register stamped with its map's Lamport time (a shared map's values) |
| `RGA` | `sequence/rga.rs` | Replicated growable array (sequence) |
| `YATA` | `sequence/yata.rs` | Collaborative-text sequence |

### Declaring a shared type

A replicated type is declared `Shared`; each field names the CRDT it converges as. The compiler
emits a `Merge` impl for the whole struct:

```logos
## Definition
A Counter is Shared and has:
    a points, which is ConvergentCount.
    a name, which is LastWriteWins of Text.

## Main
    Let c be a new Counter.
```

The field-type keywords map onto the structs above:

| Declared as | CRDT |
|-------------|------|
| `ConvergentCount` | `GCounter` |
| `a Tally` | `PNCounter` |
| `LastWriteWins of T` | `LWWRegister<T>` |
| `a Divergent T` | `MVRegister<T>` |
| `a SharedSet of T` | `ORSet<T>` |
| `a SharedSequence of T` | `RGA` |
| `a SharedMap from K to V` | `ORMap<K, LatestWrite<V>>` |

A shared map's keys are an observed-remove set (a concurrent write beats a remove) and each value a
last-writer register ordered by the map's own Lamport time: a write that has seen another write beats
it, and two concurrent writes resolve to the larger value. With no wall clock and no replica id, two
replicas that have seen the same writes hold the same map on the tree-walker, the VM and the compiled
binary; a merged map renders and iterates by key:

```logos
## Definition
A Warehouse is Shared and has:
    stock: a SharedMap from Text to Int.

## Main
Let mutable a be a new Warehouse.
Set a's stock["wood"] to 50.
Let mutable b be a new Warehouse.
Set b's stock["wood"] to 99.
Merge b into a.
Set a's stock["wood"] to 1.
Merge a into b.
Show a's stock["wood"].
Show b's stock["wood"].
```

```output
1
1
```

### Mutating and merging

Once declared, CRDT operations read naturally:

```logos
Increase local's points by 10.       # GCounter
Decrease game's score by 5.          # PNCounter
Append "Hello" to doc's lines.       # RGA sequence
Resolve page's title to "Final".     # MVRegister
Merge remote into local.
```

These are the `IncreaseCrdt`, `DecreaseCrdt`, `AppendToSequence`, `ResolveConflict` and
`MergeCrdt` statements.

`Converge remote into local.` is the idempotent lattice join (`JoinCrdt`). It differs from `Merge` on
one kind of field: a plain `Int` field takes the maximum where `Merge` adds, so a redelivered state
applied twice equals applying it once. Counter fields take the per-replica maximum under both, and
every other field folds as under `Merge`:

```logos
## Definition
A Mixed is Shared and has:
    points: ConvergentCount.
    tag: Int.

## Main
    Let mutable a be a new Mixed with tag 7.
    Increase a's points by 5.
    Let mutable b be a new Mixed with tag 2.
    Increase b's points by 3.
    Converge b into a.
    Show a's points.
    Show a's tag.
```

```output
8
7
```

With `Merge b into a.` in its place the program shows `8` and `9`.

## Networking & persistence

[`logicaffeine_system`](../crates/logicaffeine_system/README.md) provides the transports, gated by
Cargo features (`relay`, `networking`, `persistence`, `concurrency`, `http` for the `Serve` server,
the Linux-only `io-uring` engine, and `full` for every native capability but `io-uring`):

- **libp2p mesh** ([`network/`](../crates/logicaffeine_system/src/network/)): TCP + QUIC, mDNS
  discovery, request/response, and **GossipSub** pub/sub for CRDT sync.
- **Thin WebSocket relay** ([`relay.rs`](../crates/logicaffeine_system/src/relay.rs) native +
  [`relay_browser.rs`](../crates/logicaffeine_system/src/relay_browser.rs) WASM, over the shared
  [`relay_proto`](../crates/logicaffeine_system/src/relay_proto.rs)): bridges the browser to the mesh
  without libp2p. `relay::RelayHub` is the same pub/sub with no listener of its own: `largo serve` and
  a compiled site whose pages use the relay answer it at `/_relay`, the path a page dials for
  `Publish`, `When a message arrives` and a `shared on` store.

The distributed verbs tie state to the network and disk:

```logos
Listen on "/ip4/127.0.0.1/tcp/8000".
Connect to "/ip4/127.0.0.1/tcp/8000".
Sync counter on "scores".            # subscribe to a GossipSub topic; auto-publish + auto-merge
Mount counter at "data/counter.journal".   # journal to disk (WAL + snapshots)
```

These are the `Listen`, `ConnectTo`, `Sync` and `Mount` statements.

## Determinism in practice

Because scheduling is seed/trace driven, a concurrent program runs identically at a given seed on the
interpreter, the VM, the C-family tiers (host C, RISC-V, the bytecode walker, CUDA) and a
deterministic AOT build. `c_family_scheduler_conformance_lock` and `e2e_deterministic_replay` assert
that every tier prints what the tree-walker prints, and that the seed-sensitive programs show more
than one outcome across seeds, so the seed reaches the binary. A default `largo build` runs free on
tokio and is outside this guarantee. This is what makes "concurrent" and "reproducible" coexist.

A failing `largo run --interpret` is recorded as a `.replay` bundle under `target/replays/` (the
seed, the scheduling trace, the embedded source and the failure), and `largo replay <file>`
re-executes it.

## See also

- The execution tiers → [Execution & performance](execution-and-performance.md)
- The runtime, data, and system crates' own READMEs

## Where this is tested

The statement set is in [`ast/stmt.rs`](../crates/logicaffeine_language/src/ast/stmt.rs), the
runtime in [`logicaffeine_runtime`](../crates/logicaffeine_runtime/README.md), the CRDTs in
[`logicaffeine_data/src/crdt/`](../crates/logicaffeine_data/src/crdt/), and networking in
[`logicaffeine_system/src/`](../crates/logicaffeine_system/src/). Every `logos` block above is
compiled by `doc_examples`, and every output shown is what the tree-walker prints.

- Structured concurrency: `phase9_structured_concurrency`.
- Tasks, pipes and select: `interp_concurrency`, `vm_concurrency`, `phase54_concurrency`,
  `op_backend_matrix_lock`, the `e2e_concurrency` suite, and `c_family_scheduler_conformance_lock`
  (which also pins `Await h into r.` binding `nothing`).
- Agents: `phase46_agents`; unreliable sends: `send_reliability`.
- CRDTs: `phase49_crdt` and `e2e_crdt` (declaring, mutating and merging), `shared_map_all_tiers`
  (the shared map on every tier), `converge_crdt_lock` (`Converge`), and `rust_crdt_lock`
  (compiled Rust's `Merge` and `Converge` against the VM).
- Networking and persistence: `phase48_network`, `phase51_mesh`, `phase52_sync`,
  `phase53_persistence`.
- Determinism: `replay_executor_port_lock` holds the deterministic build's executor to the
  runtime's scheduler, `e2e_deterministic_replay` holds those binaries to the tree-walker and the VM,
  and `replay_lock` holds `.replay` capture and `largo replay`.

# Execution & performance

You should not have to pick between a sub-second edit loop and a compiled binary, so LOGOS puts
several back-ends behind one front-end. A program can be interpreted for instant feedback, run on
a bytecode VM that tiers up to native machine code, compiled ahead-of-time to Rust, emitted
directly as a self-contained WebAssembly module, or lowered to C, RISC-V, CUDA and accelerator
targets. The VM with its JIT is benchmarked against V8, and the compiled Rust tier against C and
the rest of a cross-language suite. Every other target is held by its own lock to the VM's
answers, or, for a modeled target, to its own contract.

After this guide you will know which tier runs your program, how to steer the optimizer from the
source, and what keeps the tiers in agreement.

## The five execution tiers

| Tier | Where | Target | Notes |
|------|-------|--------|-------|
| **Tree-walking interpreter** | [`interpreter.rs`](../crates/logicaffeine_compile/src/interpreter.rs) | native + WASM | Direct AST evaluation; sub-second feedback (`largo run --interpret`) |
| **Bytecode VM** | [`vm/`](../crates/logicaffeine_compile/src/vm/) (`compiler.rs`, `machine.rs`) | native + WASM | Register-based; portable; JIT-eligible; the browser engine |
| **Copy-and-patch JIT (EXODIA)** | [`forge/`](../crates/logicaffeine_forge/) + [`jit/`](../crates/logicaffeine_jit/) | x86-64 System V (Linux, macOS) | Tiers up from hot VM functions/loops (`vm/native_tier.rs`); elsewhere the VM runs bytecode |
| **AOT Rust codegen** | [`codegen/`](../crates/logicaffeine_compile/src/codegen/) | native + WASM | The tier benchmarked against C and the cross-language suite (`largo build`) |
| **Direct WASM backend** | [`vm/wasm/`](../crates/logicaffeine_compile/src/vm/wasm/) | WebAssembly | Emits a self-contained `.wasm` module with no `rustc`/`cargo`/`wasm-bindgen` in the loop — milliseconds (`largo build --emit wasm`); `--emit wasm-linked` links the real Rust runtime via `rust-lld` for exact arbitrary-precision integers and the exact extension's values |

Serving HTTP is one of the places the tiers meet. A `Serve` statement runs on the interpreter,
the bytecode virtual machine and the compiled Rust tier, and a differential lock holds the three
byte-identical: they answer the same request with the same bytes. They share one production
lifecycle (bounded admission, body and read-deadline caps, graceful drain) read from one place. It
is refused on the device backends, which have no host sockets. See [Web](web.md).

## Other targets

Beside the tiers, `largo emit <target>` writes the program for another machine; the
[CLI guide](cli.md) lists every target's flags and output files. The lock named in each row holds the
target to the VM, or a modeled target to its own contract. The halves that execute an artifact need
that target's toolchain or device (a C compiler, `qemu-riscv64`, `nvcc` and a GPU, TT-Metalium,
ngspice, the Spatial toolchain). `op_backend_matrix_lock` classifies every bytecode op against C,
Rust, RISC-V, WASM, CUDA, Tenstorrent and the spatial fabric and holds each backend to a coverage
floor. A program the exact extension reaches runs on C, linked WebAssembly and RISC-V, which link the
extension's value runtime beside it; the Silicon ISA, CUDA, Tenstorrent, analog, Plasticine and RDU tiers
refuse one by name, since nothing they run on can call that runtime (`exact_on_devices_lock`).

| Target | Where | Command | Notes |
|--------|-------|---------|-------|
| **C** | [`codegen_c/`](../crates/logicaffeine_compile/src/codegen_c/) | `largo emit c` | One self-contained C file with its runtime embedded; a general backend, described below the table (`c_numeric_tower_lock`, `crdt_backend_lock`) |
| **RISC-V** | [`codegen_riscv/`](../crates/logicaffeine_compile/src/codegen_riscv/) | `largo emit riscv`, `largo build --emit riscv` | RV64GC assembly plus a small C runtime (`logos_rt.c`); link with a RISC-V GCC, run under `qemu-riscv64` (`riscv_aot_lock`). A program the exact extension reaches also links that extension's value runtime, built for RISC-V and linked statically (`exact_on_riscv_lock`) |
| **Silicon ISA** | [`vm/isa.rs`](../crates/logicaffeine_compile/src/vm/isa.rs) | `largo build --emit isa` | The register-VM opcode set as a chip ISA listing, every instruction tagged with its reversibility class, written as `<entry>.isa` (`isa_aot_lock`) |
| **WASM DOM** | [`vm/wasm/`](../crates/logicaffeine_compile/src/vm/wasm/) | `largo emit wasm-dom` | A self-contained `.wasm` page plus the `.html`/`.js` host that wires its `dom_*` imports to the browser (see [Frontend](frontend.md)); the page's DOM operations match the tree-walker's and the VM's (`wasm_dom`, `wasm_dom_emit`) |
| **CUDA** | [`codegen_cuda/`](../crates/logicaffeine_compile/src/codegen_cuda/) | `largo emit cuda` | One `.cu` running the whole program on one GPU thread (the C tier's body lifted to `__device__`), a host launcher, a `Makefile` and the C oracle it is checked against; a concurrent program runs on the stepped scheduler (`cuda_aot_lock`). Tensor sentences also lower to parallel GPU kernels through the library entry points |
| **Tenstorrent** | [`codegen_tt/`](../crates/logicaffeine_compile/src/codegen_tt/) | `largo emit tenstorrent` | A single-Tensix-core TT-Metalium program: the C tier's compute body as a kernel on one baby RISC-V core, a host orchestrator, CMake glue and the C oracle. Tasks, pipes, select and sleep are refused (`tenstorrent_aot_lock`) |
| **Analog** | [`codegen_ana/`](../crates/logicaffeine_compile/src/codegen_ana/) | `largo emit analog` | A modeled mixed-signal bundle for a float-dataflow region: tile netlist, gain schedule, range certificate, itemized error budget and a behavioral ngspice netlist; an integer-only program is refused (`analog_target_lock`) |
| **Plasticine** | [`codegen_sva/`](../crates/logicaffeine_compile/src/codegen_sva/) | `largo emit plasticine` | A counted loop as Spatial source for the open RDU toolchain, a regression app checking the VM's answer, a placement and a modeled report (`emit_plasticine`) |
| **RDU** | [`spatial/`](../crates/logicaffeine_compile/src/spatial/) | `largo emit rdu` | The SambaNova RDU lane chosen by program shape (tensor, loop or whole program): a certified neutral placement, its certificate and a modeled report; vendor configuration is gated on the vendor SDK (`emit_rdu_lanes`) |

**The C backend.** `largo emit c` writes one self-contained C file carrying the stdlib prelude and
the exact numeric tower: an `Int` promotes to a big integer on provable overflow, in growing
accumulators and in every `**`, beside rationals, complex and modular values. It also carries money,
quantities, UUIDs, words and temporal values, collections, records and enums, CRDT counters, and
concurrency on the ported scheduler ([Concurrency](concurrency.md)). Where C cannot prove an
`Int`'s operands bounded, its arithmetic wraps; that divergence is ledgered in
[`c_known_divergences.txt`](../crates/logicaffeine_tests/tests/gauntlet/c_known_divergences.txt). A
Rust-only native kernel, or a CRDT kind C does not lower, is refused by name.

The multi-core and accelerator lowerings (Tensix meshes, the persistent CUDA kernel, the
reconfigurable fabric and the RDU) are backends of one spatial IR
([`spatial/`](../crates/logicaffeine_compile/src/spatial/)): stages over bounded buffers joined by
typed handshakes and placed on a described mesh. Each lowering refuses by name what it cannot
place. The
[`codegen_sva/`](../crates/logicaffeine_compile/src/codegen_sva/) module is also English →
SystemVerilog Assertions and runtime monitors for hardware verification (see
[Proof & verification](proof-and-verification.md)), and generates Verilog RTL for the hardware
targets: the soft cores, the reconfigurable fabric and the whole-program engine.

## How tier-up works

The VM runs bytecode. When a function or loop gets hot, **EXODIA**, the copy-and-patch JIT
(`ForgeTier`, installed via [`logicaffeine_jit::install`](../crates/logicaffeine_jit/src/lib.rs)),
compiles it to native machine code by stitching pre-built stencils together and patching in the
live operands, so compilation stays fast and execution is native. A register-allocating x86-64
backend (`regalloc.rs`) sits above per-stencil dispatch. JIT regions carry **deoptimization
guards**: if a region sees data it didn't specialize for, it bails safely back to bytecode. Set
`LOGOS_NO_JIT` to stay on the VM. (`vm/native_tier.rs`, `vm/aot_tier.rs`.)

In the browser, the interpreter and VM run in WebAssembly and produce byte-identical results to
native; that is what powers the in-page [Studio](studio-and-learn.md). The direct WASM backend is
the complement: instead of running the engine *in* WASM, it compiles the program *to* a WASM module
(locked to VM/interpreter behavior by the `wasm_aot_lock` differentials); the `wasm-jit` feature
additionally lets JIT'd hot regions execute in-browser (`vm/wasm/region_jit.rs`).

## The optimizer

Optimizations are registry-driven. Each pass is registered in
[`logicaffeine_language/src/optimization.rs`](../crates/logicaffeine_language/src/optimization.rs)
(`REGISTRY`, one row per optimization: its keyword, the paths it touches, its cost, whether it emits
`unsafe`, and what it requires, conflicts with and preempts) and toggled through a single
`OptimizationConfig`. The passes themselves live in
[`compile/src/optimize/`](../crates/logicaffeine_compile/src/optimize/) and the code generators in
[`codegen/`](../crates/logicaffeine_compile/src/codegen/), covering bounds-check elimination, loop
transforms, scalarization, de-`Rc`, inlining, dense-map specialization, and more.

Source decorators select them by keyword, and every tier's compile path honors them: AOT-Rust
(`largo build`, `largo emit rust`), C, the VM, WASM and the Silicon ISA.

| Decorator | Effect |
|-----------|--------|
| `## No <keyword>` | Turns the optimization off for the function that follows, or program-wide when it sits before `## Main`; `## No Optimize` turns every one off |
| `## Require <keyword>` | Compilation fails, naming the keyword, when the optimization did not fire for the program, so a dependence on an optimization becomes an error. `largo run --interpret` refuses it up front: the check belongs to the compiled path (`largo run`, `largo build`, `largo emit`) |
| `## Tier <keyword> <pin>` | Pins the hotness tier at which the run path's tiered optimizer pays for it: `eager`, `never`, or a tier `t0`–`t3`. `## No` wins over any pin |

An unknown keyword is ignored. The ambient equivalents are `LOGOS_OPT_OFF=<kw>,<kw>` (and
`LOGOS_OPT=off` for all), and `LOGOS_TIER_PIN=<kw>:<pin>,…`, which a `## Tier` decorator overrides.
The keywords, in the groups the registry files them under (the headings `largo opts` prints):

| Group | Keywords |
|-------|----------|
| Inlining & calls | `memo`, `tco`, `specialize`, `comptime`, `inline`, `unfold`, `defunctionalize`, `foldfuse` |
| Peephole | `peephole` |
| Arrays & memory | `borrow`, `scalarize`, `affine`, `interleave`, `unbox`, `hoistborrows`, `regpromote`, `variantbox`, `bitpack`, `stridefill` |
| Loops | `loophoist`, `unroll`, `loopsplit`, `closedform`, `fuse`, `loopcse`, `interchange`, `tile`, `accumbound`, `divmodfuse`, `specializeloop`, `sortnest`, `divisorsieve`, `tracememo` |
| Redundancy | `cse`, `deadcode`, `sccp`, `probefuse` |
| Number representation | `narrow`, `narrowvm`, `narrowmap`, `densemap`, `elemtype`, `fastdiv`, `floatstrength`, `intstrength` |
| Bounds & checks | `oracle`, `oraclehints`, `unchecked`, `hintversion` |
| Strings & SIMD | `simd`, `cascade`, `indexstring`, `capscale`, `asciiclassmask` |
| Search-space | `symmetry`, `popcount`, `saturate`, `supercompile` |
| Bignum | `bignumbyref`, `bignuminplace` |
| Bits | `bitintrinsics` |
| Text | `textbytesview`, `stringaccumreuse`, `textfrombytesbuilder`, `textslicereturn`, `stringconcatreuse`, `stringrepeatloop`, `radixdigitbuffer` |
| Math | `simdreduce` |
| Arithmetic | `strengthreducepow2`, `branchlessaccumulate`, `wideaccumulator`, `masknarrow`, `modwrap`, `branchlessselect` |
| Bytes | `byteslicereturn` |

```logos
## Require memo

## To fib (n: Int) -> Int:
    If n is less than 2:
        Return n.
    Return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2).

## Main
Show fib(10).
```

Memoization fires on the double recursion, so this compiles; the same decorator over a program with
nothing to memoize is a compile error.

To see exactly which optimizations *fired* for a program:

```bash
largo opts src/main.lg          # human-readable
largo opts src/main.lg --json   # keyword list
```

## Benchmarks

The [`benchmarks/`](../benchmarks/) directory holds the harness and recorded results
([`benchmarks/results/`](../benchmarks/results/)); its [README](../benchmarks/README.md) explains how
each suite runs and the fairness rules every implementation follows. LOGOS is measured two ways:

- **AOT**: `largo build --release` against C, C++, Rust, Zig, Go, Java, JavaScript, Python, Ruby
  and Nim on a shared set of programs, every output verified before anything is timed.
- **VM + JIT**: `largo run --interpret` against Node.js (V8), both running the same naive
  algorithm, to track the non-compiled path.

The current charts are in the root README's [Benchmarks](../README.md#benchmarks) section,
regenerated from the JSON under `benchmarks/results/`, and the interactive suite is on the
[`/benchmarks`](https://logicaffeine.com/benchmarks) page. This guide quotes no figures, because
they move with every optimization. One distinction to read them with: where the optimizer proves a
shortcut, compiled LOGOS skips work that C still executes, so the charts report those programs
apart from the same-algorithm comparisons.

## Verifying the compiler itself

Three mechanisms keep the tiers honest:

- **Differential tests** (`e2e_differential`, `e2e_feature_matrix`) assert the tree-walker, the VM
  and the compiled Rust agree on output; `op_backend_matrix_lock` and the per-target locks above
  extend the same contract to every other backend.
- **Tier divergence as a verdict.** `tier_differential` runs a program on the tree-walker and the VM
  and classifies any disagreement as a compiler bug with a ready-to-file reproduction
  (`tier_divergence_drill`); `largo test --tiers all` applies it to every passing `## Test`.
- **Translation validation** ([`logicaffeine_tv`](../crates/logicaffeine_tv/README.md)) symbolically
  executes the LOGOS source into bitvector/boolean terms and proves with Z3 that the encoding agrees
  with the tree-walker on the ordered `Show` outputs and the error outcome, over straight-line
  `Int`/`Bool` programs and a determinate concurrency fragment. The emitted-Rust side of the
  equivalence has no symbolic executor, so source ↔ emitted-Rust equivalence is not closed.

## See also

- The language being executed → [Imperative mode](imperative-mode.md)
- The crate layout and gating → [Architecture](architecture.md)

## Where this is tested

The execution tiers live in [`crates/logicaffeine_compile/src/`](../crates/logicaffeine_compile/src/),
the JIT in [`crates/logicaffeine_forge/`](../crates/logicaffeine_forge/README.md) and
[`crates/logicaffeine_jit/`](../crates/logicaffeine_jit/README.md), and the harness in
[`benchmarks/`](../benchmarks/). Each target's lock is named in its table row above, and
`op_backend_matrix_lock` holds every backend to its coverage floor. `decorator_through_largo`
holds the optimization decorators on the real `largo` compile path and on the C, ISA and WASM
compilers, and `e2e_require_optimization` holds `## Require` to failing when its optimization does
not fire.

SOURCE: docs/proof-and-verification.md — Proof & verification
